title: Potty Training Is Not the State's Responsibility
author: Daisy Mae Inglese
summary: Responding to a BBC News report that a potty training scheme is being rolled out to 20 more areas of the UK, Daisy Mae Inglese argues that the State is taking over a duty that belongs to parents. She grants that there is a real crisis of childhood independence, citing teachers' reports that one in four children start school unable to use the toilet independently. But she contends the deeper cause is a culture in which parents have drifted into dependence on government-funded childcare and welfare, and in which mothers returning to work hand babies to strangers. Disposable diapers and the marketing of Big Diaper play a part, she says, but cannot explain a shift from toilet training at 15 to 18 months in the 1950s. Her larger point is that the family is the sphere of the private and the State the sphere of the common, so surrendering basic child-rearing to government erodes the liberty that depends on capable families.
points: Inglese concedes the problem is real, since staff are losing teaching time to basic caregiving for children who start school unprepared.
She locates the root cause in parents reneging on a fundamental duty and in State incentives that encourage dependence and outsourced child-rearing.
The historical contrast of 1950s potty training at 15 to 18 months against today's later ages is used to show that diaper marketing alone cannot explain the change.
She distinguishes providing financially for children from the duty to rear them and cultivate their independence at the right age.
The closing argument is political: if the family's duties are handed to the State, there is no domain of life the State should not govern.
quotes: We face a genuine crisis of childhood independence. Teachers report that one in four children in the UK start school unable to go to the bathroom independently.
Teaching children to use the toilet was simply part of a parent’s duty, no different from teaching them to speak or to walk.
Yet in the 1950s, the average age for potty training was between 15-18 months

Such close attention becomes impossible in Western societies where mothers have returned to work, leaving their babies in the care of strangers who have little reason to invest themselves in the intricacies of each child’s development.
The West has forgotten the sacredness of family life as a vocation, and the responsibilities it entails may now seem too great for many who choose to undertake it.
Providing financially for your children is undoubtedly important, but it must never be conflated with the duty to rear them and cultivate their independence at the right age and time.
We once understood that the family, with its sacred duties and responsibilities, is the sphere of the private, while the State is that of the public or common.
If we surrender the responsibilities of family life to the State, as if it is better equipped to fulfill them, is there any domain of our lives the State should not govern?
